subject: Ch6: Semantic Analysis & Syntax-Directed Translation (Hard)
description: Hard-level MCQs on syntax-directed definitions and translation schemes, synthesized/inherited attributes, S- and L-attributed grammars, dependency graphs and evaluation order, type checking and type equivalence, symbol tables and scope, and intermediate forms (AST, DAG, three-address code).

questions.text: In the SDD rule for D → T L with L.inh := T.type, the attribute L.inh is:
options: a terminal attribute attached directly to a token produced by the lexical analyzer rather than to a nonterminal
synthesized, because its value is computed by combining the attributes of L's own children further down in the tree
inherited, passed down from the parent or a left sibling such as T, since its value originates above or to its left in the production rather than from its own subtree
undefined, since the production assigns no meaningful value to the left-hand nonterminal D in this rule
questions.shortExplanation: Value flows down from sibling T → inherited.
questions.explanation: L.inh takes its value from T (a left sibling) above in the production, so it flows downward — the defining trait of an inherited attribute.

questions.text: A syntax-directed definition is S-attributed if it uses:
options: only synthesized attributes, meaning every attribute value is computed solely from the attributes of a node's children and therefore flows strictly upward during a bottom-up parse
both synthesized and inherited attributes together, with completely arbitrary dependencies allowed among them
only inherited attributes, each one obtaining its value strictly from the parent node and the left siblings in the production
no attributes whatsoever on any of the grammar symbols appearing in the productions
questions.shortExplanation: S-attributed = purely synthesized.
questions.explanation: An S-attributed SDD has only synthesized attributes, so all values flow upward and can be computed during a bottom-up parse.

questions.text: Every S-attributed SDD is also L-attributed because:
options: the L-attributed restriction, which constrains only inherited attributes, is automatically satisfied when an SDD has no inherited attributes at all
the L-attributed class explicitly forbids any use of synthesized attributes anywhere in the productions
it necessarily contains inherited attributes whose definitions depend on the synthesized attributes of their right siblings, which an L-attributed scheme would explicitly require for correctness
synthesized attributes are computed from values passed downward by the parent
questions.shortExplanation: No inherited attrs ⇒ L-attributed condition holds vacuously.
questions.explanation: L-attributed only constrains inherited attributes (parent and left siblings); with none present, an S-attributed SDD trivially qualifies as L-attributed.

questions.text: Which inherited-attribute dependency VIOLATES the L-attributed condition?
options: B.inh depends on a left symbol's synthesized attribute
C.inh depends on the attribute of its right sibling D, drawing a value from a symbol that has not yet been processed in a left-to-right traversal
the head of the production synthesizes its own attribute value purely from the attributes of its children, which is a perfectly ordinary synthesized dependency and not an inherited one at all
B.inh depends on the inherited attribute of the parent symbol A appearing on the left-hand side of the production, a permitted upward-context dependency in any L-attributed scheme
questions.shortExplanation: Depending on a RIGHT sibling breaks L-attributed.
questions.explanation: L-attributed inherited attributes may depend only on the parent and LEFT siblings; a dependency on a right sibling makes a left-to-right pass impossible.

questions.text: A dependency graph for an annotated parse tree must be acyclic so that:
options: the underlying context-free grammar can be guaranteed to be unambiguous for every input string it accepts
the FOLLOW sets of all the grammar's nonterminals become well-defined and computable
the resulting parse tree is forced to take a strictly binary shape at every interior node
a topological order of the nodes exists in which to evaluate every attribute, guaranteeing that each value is computed only after all the attributes it depends upon are already available
questions.shortExplanation: Acyclic ⇒ topological evaluation order exists.
questions.explanation: Attribute evaluation follows a topological sort of the dependency graph; a cycle would mean no consistent order, making evaluation impossible.

questions.text: Semantic actions for an S-attributed definition are conventionally placed:
options: at the very beginning of each production, before any of the right-hand-side grammar symbols have been parsed, so that the action runs ahead of every child and its subtree
somewhere in the middle of each production, interleaved between the right-hand-side grammar symbols
at the end of each production, so that all of the children's synthesized attribute values have already been computed and are ready for use when the action executes
exclusively within the start-symbol production
questions.shortExplanation: Synthesized values are computed at the right end.
questions.explanation: Because synthesized attributes use children's values, the action is placed at the production's right end, matching a reduction in bottom-up parsing.

questions.text: To evaluate an L-attributed SDD during top-down parsing, embedded actions for an inherited attribute of a symbol are placed:
options: immediately before that symbol in the right-hand side of the production, so that the inherited attribute is computed and made available just in time, before the parser begins to expand that symbol and its subtree
in a completely separate traversal pass that walks over the parse tree after the main parse finishes
immediately after that symbol, once it and all of its descendants in the parse tree have been fully processed
at the very end of the production only, after every right-hand-side symbol has already been parsed
questions.shortExplanation: Inherited attrs must be set before the symbol is parsed.
questions.explanation: Since an inherited attribute must be available when its symbol is processed, the computing action is placed just before that symbol in the right-hand side.

questions.text: Under STRUCTURAL type equivalence, the types `Point = record{x:int; y:int}` and `Coord = record{x:int; y:int}` are:
options: equivalent only on the condition that both records happen to be declared inside the very same declaration block

equivalent, because under structural equivalence two types are the same whenever their type expressions have identical shape, and here both records have exactly the same fields x:int and y:int in the same order
never comparable at all, since records with named fields lie outside the type system's equivalence relation
different, because the two record types were introduced under two distinct type names in the program
questions.shortExplanation: Same structure ⇒ structurally equivalent.
questions.explanation: Structural equivalence ignores names and compares the type expressions' shapes; identical field structure makes Point and Coord equivalent.

questions.text: Under NAME type equivalence, those same two record types are:
options: equivalent after a coercion converts one into the other
equivalent, since name equivalence compares the internal field structure of the two records and finds them identical
equivalent as long as the fields of the two records match in their names, order, and individual types, which is precisely what name equivalence is defined to check
distinct, because name equivalence treats each separately declared type name as its own type, so Point and Coord differ
questions.shortExplanation: Different names ⇒ distinct under name equivalence.
questions.explanation: Name equivalence treats each distinct type name as a different type, so Point and Coord are not equivalent regardless of structure.

questions.text: A widening coercion inserted for `intVar + floatVar` is recorded by the type checker as:
options: an implicit widening conversion that promotes the int operand to a float value first, so the addition is then carried out entirely in floating-point arithmetic
a reduction step the parser performs on the production
a brand-new token spliced into the input stream
a syntax error that the parser should have rejected long before the expression ever reached the type checker, since mixed-type arithmetic is forbidden by the grammar's production rules themselves
questions.shortExplanation: Type checker inserts int→float widening.
questions.explanation: The type checker resolves the mixed-mode operation by coercing the int to float (widening), producing a float addition; this is implicit conversion.

questions.text: Which intermediate form is BEST for exposing and sharing common subexpressions?
options: A directed acyclic graph (DAG), in which every repeated subexpression is represented by a single shared node that the duplicate occurrences all point to, making the common subexpressions explicit
A regular expression describing the lexical pattern of the identifiers used in the expression
The raw token stream produced by the lexical analyzer before any parsing has taken place
A full parse tree, which faithfully records every derivation step taken by the grammar during parsing
questions.shortExplanation: DAG shares identical subexpressions via one node.
questions.explanation: A DAG reuses a single node for each repeated subexpression, making common-subexpression sharing explicit, unlike a tree which duplicates them.

questions.text: A symbol table for a block-structured language is commonly implemented as a stack of scopes so that:
options: an identifier, once declared, can never be redeclared
the compiler can avoid tracking any scope information at all while still resolving every name correctly
every identifier lookup is forced to scan the entire program text from beginning to end before it can succeed
entering a block pushes a new scope and leaving it pops, giving correct nested visibility
questions.shortExplanation: Push/pop scopes model nested block visibility.
questions.explanation: A scope stack lets inner declarations shadow outer ones; on block exit the scope is popped, restoring the enclosing scope's visibility.

questions.text: Three-address code differs from a syntax tree mainly in that three-address code:
options: stores only operands and discards every operator
cannot represent assignment statements at all
names each intermediate result with an explicit temporary variable, thereby flattening the nested expression into a linear sequence of simple instructions
is exactly the same sequence of symbols as the token stream emitted by the lexical analyzer, with no further processing applied to it whatsoever beyond scanning
questions.shortExplanation: TAC linearizes with explicit temporaries.
questions.explanation: Three-address code breaks expressions into a sequence of instructions, each with up to three operands and an explicit temporary for each subresult.

questions.text: In `t1 = b * c; t2 = a + t1`, the use of temporaries reflects that the original expression was:
options: a + b + c, associating left to right
a * b + c, multiplying the first two operands a and b together and then adding the third operand c to that product to obtain the final result
a + b * c, where the multiplication b*c binds more tightly than the addition and so is computed into the temporary t1 first
(a + b) * c, where the explicit parentheses force the addition a+b to be evaluated first, before the result is multiplied by the operand c
questions.shortExplanation: b*c computed first ⇒ a + b*c.
questions.explanation: Because b*c (t1) is formed before adding a, the precedence shows the source was a + b * c, where multiplication has higher precedence.

questions.text: Why are synthesized attributes naturally evaluated by an LR (bottom-up) parser?
options: Because LR parsers cannot compute attributes at all
Because each synthesized attribute is defined using its parent's inherited attributes
Because computing them correctly always demands a second, completely separate traversal over the finished parse tree once the entire bottom-up parse has already run to completion
Because their values are derived from the attributes of a node's children, and in bottom-up parsing those children are reduced before the parent node is, so the values are already on hand
questions.shortExplanation: Children reduce first, so their synthesized values are ready.
questions.explanation: In bottom-up parsing a production is reduced after its right-hand symbols, so the children's synthesized attributes are available to compute the parent's.

questions.text: An inherited attribute is genuinely needed (synthesized alone won't do) when information must flow:
options: from the scanner directly to the linker, bypassing the parser and the semantic analyzer in between
from the children of a node upward into the parent, summarizing what the subtree has computed
from a declaration's type down to identifiers, i.e., context flowing into a subtree
out of the parse process entirely and into a wholly separate analysis phase of the compiler
questions.shortExplanation: Context flowing INTO a subtree needs inherited attributes.
questions.explanation: When a subtree needs context determined elsewhere (e.g., a declared type applied to a list of names), that downward/contextual flow requires inherited attributes.

questions.text: Which is a SEMANTIC (not syntactic) error?
options: Assigning a string value to a variable that was declared with integer type, which is well-formed syntactically but violates the language's type-compatibility rules during checking
A missing closing brace that leaves a compound statement block unbalanced in the source program, so the parser cannot match the opening delimiter and reports a structural grammar violation
A stray '@' character appearing where the lexical rules permit no such symbol at all
An unterminated string literal that runs to the end of the line without a matching closing quote, which the scanner flags as a malformed token during lexical analysis before parsing even begins
questions.shortExplanation: Type mismatch is semantic.
questions.explanation: A type-incompatible assignment violates the language's type rules (semantics); the others are lexical or syntactic problems.

questions.text: A type expression for a function from integers to booleans is best written as:
options: integer × boolean, denoting a Cartesian product of the integer type and the boolean type
integer → boolean, using the arrow type constructor whose left side is the integer domain type and whose right side is the boolean result type returned by the function
pointer(integer), denoting a pointer that refers to a storage cell holding an integer
array(boolean), denoting an array whose elements are each of the boolean type
questions.shortExplanation: Function type uses the → constructor.
questions.explanation: Function types use the arrow constructor: integer → boolean denotes a function taking an integer and returning a boolean.

questions.text: Postfix notation produced by an SDD for expressions is generated by emitting an operator:
options: in the place of its operands entirely, replacing them rather than following or preceding them
after the actions that emit its operands (a postorder action)
before evaluating any of its operands, so the operator symbol is printed ahead of its arguments
only once at the root of the whole expression tree, after the entire input has been consumed
questions.shortExplanation: Emit operator after operands (postorder).
questions.explanation: Placing the print action for an operator after the operand actions yields postfix output, matching a postorder traversal of the expression tree.

questions.text: An SDD whose attributes can be evaluated in a single left-to-right depth-first traversal corresponds exactly to the class of:
options: ambiguous grammars
L-attributed definitions, whose inherited attributes depend only on the parent and on left siblings, all of which are already computed when a single left-to-right depth-first walk reaches the node

S-attributed definitions only, which are strictly restricted to purely synthesized attributes that flow upward and thus could never accommodate any inherited attribute at all during such a single depth-first traversal of the tree

regular grammars, whose productions are limited to the right-linear or left-linear forms and therefore generate only the regular languages that are recognizable by some finite automaton with no auxiliary memory
questions.shortExplanation: Single left-to-right pass ⇔ L-attributed.
questions.explanation: L-attributed SDDs are precisely those evaluable in one depth-first left-to-right traversal, since inherited attributes use only already-computed parent/left-sibling values.

questions.text: When checking a function call f(a, b), the type checker must verify the number AND types of arguments against:
options: the FOLLOW set of the call construct, which lists the terminals that may legally follow it
f's declared parameter (signature) information in the symbol table
the depth at which the call expression happens to appear inside the program's full parse tree
the FIRST set of the nonterminal that derives the function name f within the grammar's productions
questions.shortExplanation: Compare actuals against the declared signature.
questions.explanation: The symbol table stores f's parameter list/return type; the checker matches the actual arguments' count and types against this signature.

questions.text: A circular dependency among attributes in an SDD means:
options: no valid evaluation order exists; the SDD is ill-defined for that tree
every attribute appearing in the dependency cycle must therefore be a synthesized attribute
the underlying grammar is necessarily ambiguous and admits multiple parse trees for some input
the evaluator simply re-runs the rules repeatedly until all the attribute values converge to a stable point
questions.shortExplanation: Cyclic dependencies ⇒ no evaluation order.
questions.explanation: If attribute A needs B and B needs A (directly or transitively), the dependency graph has a cycle and there is no consistent order to compute them.

questions.text: Which statement about abstract syntax trees (ASTs) versus parse trees is TRUE?
options: An AST retains every nonterminal node together with all the punctuation and separator tokens from the source, faithfully mirroring every step of the grammar's derivation
A parse tree omits operators, recording only the operands that appear at the leaves of the derivation, so the structure loses all of the arithmetic and logical operation symbols
An AST drops grammar-only nodes, keeping operators and operands
An AST and a parse tree are always structurally identical for any given input program without exception, regardless of how the grammar happens to be written
questions.shortExplanation: AST condenses, removing grammar-only nodes.
questions.explanation: An AST abstracts away derivation artifacts (e.g., E→T→F chains, parentheses, commas), retaining the essential operator/operand structure.

questions.text: In a YACC action `E : E '+' T { $$ = $1 + $3; }`, $3 refers to:
options: the value of T (the third grammar symbol on the right)
the semantic value carried by the '+' terminal token sitting between the two operands in the rule
the next production that the parser will attempt to apply once this reduction has finished
the semantic value of the E nonterminal appearing on the left-hand side of this very production
questions.shortExplanation: $3 = third RHS symbol = T.
questions.explanation: Right-hand-side symbols are numbered left to right: $1=E, $2='+', $3=T; so $3 is T's semantic value.

questions.text: Static (lexical) scoping resolves a free variable reference by searching:
options: the symbol table maintained by the linker while it combines the separately compiled object modules
the chain of procedure calls that happen to be active on the run-time stack at the moment of the reference
the textually enclosing scopes at compile time
the FOLLOW set of the deriving nonterminal
questions.shortExplanation: Lexical scope ⇒ search enclosing program text.
questions.explanation: Static scoping binds a name to the declaration found in the nearest textually enclosing scope, determined at compile time, not by run-time call order.

questions.text: The MOST appropriate place to detect a 'variable used before declaration' error is:
options: lexical analysis, while the scanner is still grouping the raw characters of the source into tokens
code generation, at the stage where target machine instructions are emitted for each operation
linking, once all of the separately compiled object files are being combined into one executable
semantic analysis using the symbol table
questions.shortExplanation: Symbol-table-based check during semantic analysis.
questions.explanation: Determining that a name has no prior declaration requires symbol-table lookups, which is the job of semantic analysis.

questions.text: Which evaluation strategy works for ANY non-circular SDD, even one that is neither S- nor L-attributed?
options: No evaluation is possible at all for such an SDD by any known systematic method whatsoever
A single bottom-up pass reducing each production once
A single top-down pass that predicts and expands productions from the start symbol downward only
Build the dependency graph and evaluate in topological order
questions.shortExplanation: Topological-order evaluation handles any acyclic SDD.
questions.explanation: For arbitrary acyclic dependencies, constructing the dependency graph and evaluating in a topological order always works, though it may need multiple passes.

questions.text: A translation scheme differs from a syntax-directed definition in that a translation scheme:
options: applies only to regular grammars
specifies the exact position and ordering of the semantic actions embedded among the grammar symbols within each production, thereby fixing precisely when each action executes
carries no semantic rules and lists only the productions
is fundamentally prohibited from making any use of synthesized attributes within its embedded actions, restricting it to inherited attributes that are passed strictly downward from parent to child
questions.shortExplanation: Schemes fix action ordering inside productions.
questions.explanation: An SDD states rules declaratively; a translation scheme additionally pins down WHERE actions execute among the symbols, fixing evaluation order.

questions.text: For the declaration list `int a, b, c;`, an inherited attribute is used to:
options: synthesize and report the total count of identifiers that appear within the declaration list
carry the type 'int' down to each of a, b, and c
emit the target machine code for a loop that would iterate over the three declared variables
compute the FOLLOW set of the nonterminal L that derives the identifier list in this grammar
questions.shortExplanation: Type 'int' is inherited by each identifier.
questions.explanation: The type from the declaration head is passed (inherited) down the identifier list so every name in the list receives type int in the symbol table.

questions.text: Overload resolution (choosing which `+` or which `print` to use based on argument types) is performed during:
options: linking only, when separate object modules are resolved
loading, when the OS brings the image into memory
lexical analysis, while the scanner is still converting the raw character stream into individual tokens long before any type information about the operands has been determined
semantic analysis, specifically the type-checking phase, where operand and argument types are consulted to select the correct overloaded operator or function definition
questions.shortExplanation: Overloading is resolved by the type checker.
questions.explanation: Selecting among overloaded operators/functions depends on operand types, so it is done during semantic analysis (type checking), using symbol-table signatures.
